items.body:
CTV News is your Alberta Referendum headquarters. Live results. Expert analysis. Everything you need to know is here.

Voting is now underway in the Alberta referendum as people head to the polls to answer 10 questions, including whether the province should stay in Canada or have another vote to separate.

More than one million people have already voted via mail-in ballots and advance voting. Polls were originally scheduled to stay open until 8 p.m. MT / 10 p.m. ET but Elections Alberta says some polls will stay open until 10 p.m. MT / 12 a.m. ET because of delays earlier in the day.

The first five questions ask about immigrants to Alberta and their access to health care, education and citizenship.

The next four ask about Alberta’s constitutional and judicial power in the country.

The final question asks if the province should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on separating.

Elections Alberta will begin to count mail-in ballots and advance votes at 5 p.m. local time, and it will begin to announce results when polls close.

Results for Question 10, or the separation question, are expected to be announced between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. local time on Tuesday, Elections Alberta said.

items._ogDesc: California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday announced the state will receive a US$6 million settlement payment in 23andMe’s bankruptcy, resolving California’s legal claims related to a 2023 data breach that exposed 6.9 million customers’ genetic and other personal information.
items.body:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday announced the state will receive a US$6 million settlement payment in 23andMe’s bankruptcy, resolving California’s legal claims related to a 2023 data breach that exposed 6.9 million customers’ genetic and other personal information.

California had unsuccessfully tried to block the US$305 million sale of 23andMe assets to TTAM Research Institute, a nonprofit controlled by 23andMe co-founder Anne Wojcicki. The state had argued that the bankruptcy sale violated California’s Genetic Information Privacy Act, and it had said consumers did not give express consent to the sale.

Once a trailblazer in DNA testing kits, 23andMe filed for bankruptcy in March 2025, seeking to sell its business at auction after a decline in demand and legal fallout from the data breach.

A U.S. bankruptcy judge ruled against California’s objections to the sale, and later ruled that the state could not sue to recover money from the bankrupt company’s successor. California lost an appeal over the sale in federal district court, and it agreed to drop further appeals as part of the US$6 million settlement, according to court documents filed on Monday.

Customers of 23andMe retained the option to delete their data during the bankruptcy sale process, but California had argued that the court should have disallowed the transfer of anydata unless 23andMe customers first gave express consent to the sale.

“I am proud to fight for the privacy rights of Californians and to deliver this settlement for consumers who put their trust in 23andMe,” Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement on Monday.

“I want to remind Californians that customers of 23andMe can delete their private, genetic data — no matter who owns it.”

The data breach exposed the genetic information of more than 855,000 Californians, according to the attorney general’s office.

23andMe agreed to pay $46.75 million to victims of the 2023 data breach as part of its bankruptcy.

(Reporting by Dietrich Knauth; Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Bill Berkrot)

Dietrich Knauth, Reuters

items.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of bugging conference room planned to fly to Saudi Arabia, prosecutors say
items.description: A former OpenAI engineer had been 'mere days' away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest last week, U.S. federal prosecutors revealed in new court filings.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Attendees gather at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in San Francisco. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jeff Chiu</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A former OpenAI engineer had been 'mere days' away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest last week, U.S. federal prosecutors revealed in new court filings.
items.body:
SAN FRANCISCO — A former OpenAI engineer charged with secretly installing a recording device in a conference room to glean company details had been “mere days” away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest last week, U.S. federal prosecutors revealed in new court filings.

Abdulrahman Alfozan’s wife and young son also left the country the day after the 35-year-old Saudi national’s arrest, travelling on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, prosecutors said in a memo Sunday seeking his continued detention.

“Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through,” federal prosecutors wrote. “He has ample resources -- including his significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area and at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia -- and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government.”

A federal judge in San Francisco sided with prosecutors Monday, denying a request by Alfozan’s lawyers to release him to home confinement. His next court date is Nov.

Alfozan’s lawyer William Pernik argued in court that his client had strong ties to the U.S. and was “weeks away from achieving every immigrant’s dream” -- U.S. citizenship.

Alfozan had a naturalization interview with federal officials scheduled next month and has been a lawful permanent resident since 2020, his lawyers said in their legal filings. He has also lived in the U.S. for 15 years and attended MIT and the University of California, Berkeley, they said.

Pernik said Alfozan is willing to put up “almost the entirety” of his assets -- about US$1 million currently in a U.S. investment account -- to cover his bond.

“Everything this man has he’s willing to surrender,” he said, adding that Alfozan’s wife is also willing to return to the U.S. as she still holds a visitor visa that expires in 2033.

Judge Alex Tse appeared doubtful, questioning whether Saudi Arabia’s government would simply reimburse Alfozan if he fled and forfeited his bond.

After the hearing, Pernik said he was disappointed with the ruling but declined further comment.

Pernik had argued in court filings that Alfozan purchased one-way tickets for his family to Saudi Arabia more than two weeks before prosecutors allege the recording devices were installed. They said the couple planned to spend Alfozan’s roughly two-month paternity leave in Saudi Arabia following the birth of their U.S.-citizen son.

But prosecutors said Saudi officials purchased new plane tickets for Alfozan’s wife and son after his arrest, allowing them to leave the U.S. sooner than the Oct. 12 flight Alfozan had originally booked.

Prosecutors have not said what Alfozan might have wanted to do with the recordings, but say he was in “frequent communication” with a member of the Saudi royal family. They said the royal family member repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan to an artificial intelligence venture being launched in Saudi Arabia.

Alfozan had told the unnamed person he wouldn’t leave OpenAI until his stock was vested, even as he explored other career opportunities in the Middle Eastern kingdom, prosecutors wrote. He had worked at the ChatGPT maker since July 2025 but was fired after his arrest.

Prosecutors say Alfozan concealed an audio recording device in toilet paper and plugged it into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room he wasn’t authorized to access. They say security cameras captured him entering the room and checking behind the television after installing the device. It remained there for several days before being found Sept. 30.

Prosecutors say the conference room was typically used for meetings involving company leaders, government officials and other executives and “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information.”

OpenAI has said the recording device Alfozan used was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities. They also said they had evidence Alfozan planned to place other listening devices elsewhere in the office.

Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a five-year prison sentence.

Marcelo reported from New York.

Barbara Ortutay and Philip Marcelo, The Associated Press

items._ogDesc: At least six miners were killed Monday when an open pit gold mine collapsed in a remote corner of Colombia’s Nariño province, authorities said.
items.body:
BOGOTA, Colombia — At least six miners were killed Monday when an open pit gold mine collapsed in a remote corner of Colombia’s Nariño province, authorities said.

Jorge Tovar Castillo, a disaster response official in Nariño, said that an additional 12 to 15 miners have been reported as missing following the accident in the municipality of Santa Barbara de Iscuande. He said that municipal authorities were handling the response to the accident but added that communication had been difficult.

Santa Barbara de Iscuande is surrounded by dense rainforest and can only be reached by boat or small aircraft.

“We are waiting for their next report,” Tovar Castillo said. “We are waiting to see if they require additional support.”

In a message on X, Nariño’s governor, Luis Alfonso Escobar, said the gold mine that collapsed was an “informal” mine.

Hundreds of small mines in Colombia operate without government permits and some are controlled by rebel groups.

“At this moment our priority is to save lives, accompany families and guarantee an opportune response to this painful tragedy,” Escobar wrote on X.

items.title: Albertans head to polls in historic referendum on whether they want to stay in Canada
items.description: Albertans head to the polls today for an historic vote on whether they want to stay in Canada.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks as Alberta Premier Danielle Smith listens in Fort McMurray on Thursday Oct 1, 2026. Prime Minister Mark Carney declared the Pacific Link pipeline project to be in the national interest. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Greg Halinda]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Albertans head to the polls today for an historic vote on whether they want to stay in Canada.
items.body:
The polls are open as Albertans mark their ballots in a historic vote on whether they want to stay in Canada.

In Calgary, voters were bustling in and out of Grace Presbyterian Church on Monday morning with their yellow “I voted” stickers before rushing off to work.

Scott Hill, donning a baseball cap with a red maple leaf, said he’s respectful of everyone’s opinion, but to him, the referendum is “surreal” and his vote was to stay.

“People are angry, I can see that. But we’re Canadian, we need to stand together,” he said, noting his grandfather fought in the Second World War.

“This is without a doubt the most important vote I’ve ever done.”

More than 1.3 million Albertans have already cast ballots by mail or in advance polls in the referendum called by Premier Danielle Smith.

They are being asked whether they want to stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

The vote caps months of rallies, speeches and analyses from both sides. It also comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney said members of Parliament are “united in grief” over a tragedy that touches every corner of the country.

A fire that ripped through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright’s training grounds in Alberta on Saturday killed four soldiers and injured dozens more.

Smith’s United Conservative Party never campaigned on holding a separation vote in the last election in 2023, but says some Albertans’ anger with the state of affairs under former Liberal prime minister Justin Trudeau has boiled over into hundreds of thousands signing petitions for and against Confederation.

A referendum, she has said, is now necessary to resolve the matter once and for all.

At the polls Monday morning in Edmonton, there was a slow-moving lineup at All Saints’ Anglican Cathedral. Jeff Sparks was one of several voters who said he hopes the remain vote wins.

“And that this puts the situation to bed and that we don’t really have to hear about this anymore,” he said.

Shawn Campbell said he voted for the province to start the process toward a binding referendum, even though he doesn’t want the province to separate, and doesn’t believe it ever will.

“It sends a message to Ottawa that Albertans are not happy,” he said.

The separation question is one of 10 on the ballot. The first nine focus on immigration and the Constitution.

The immigration questions ask Albertans whether the province should have more say on who comes to the province to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations — and perhaps introduce fees — on some who arrive and seek access to health care and education.

The constitutional questions ask Albertans for a blessing to pursue talks with other provinces on wresting power from the federal government and abolishing the Senate.

Smith has said the first nine questions are meant to give leverage in the province’s negotiations with Ottawa.

The premier has also said she voted to stay in Canada but says she needs a yes to those remaining nine questions to get a mandate to bargain for a better deal with Carney.

Amneet Mann cast a vote in Calgary, calling some of those questions anti-immigrant.

“I just don’t think that’s what this country stands for,” she said. “I think it’s crazy that we’re here and we have to make that known.”

Carney came to Alberta last week to rally the pro-Canada forces but also to agree to disagree with Smith. He urged Albertans to reject the nine remaining questions.

“(Say) no to the nine,” Carney told a Calgary crowd.

Jamie Fisher went to Mount Royal School in Calgary to vote to move forward with a binding separation referendum, and to support Smith’s other nine proposals.

“I don’t think it’s been fair for a really long time, and I think a lot people need to really hear that message,” she said.

Carney’s statement made her angry, she said.

“(It) just shows that it’s more of a dictatorship than listening to people,” she said.

“Everyone is going to have a different answer and that’s OK, but it feels good to be heard.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

— With files from Dayne Patterson in Calgary and Timon Johnson in Edmonton

items.title: ‘Felt like the right time’: Former broadcaster Pamela Wallin resigns from Senate
items.description: Pamela Wallin, a trail-blazing broadcaster and Order of Canada recipient, has resigned from the Senate.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Senator Pamela Wallin speaks at a press conference in Ottawa on Thursday, Feb. 1, 2024. THE CANADIAN PRESS/ Patrick Doyle]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">PATRICK DOYLE</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Pamela Wallin, a trail-blazing broadcaster and Order of Canada recipient, has resigned from the Senate.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Pamela Wallin knows her decision to resign from the Senate on Monday came as a surprise to some — but to her, she said, it “just felt like the right time” to move on after 17 years.

“I know people are always surprised when somebody walks away, but we all know our time,” Wallin said in an interview.

The news broke on Monday morning after a note was sent to senators from the Senate clerk and Wallin’s biography on the Senate website was changed to list her as a former member.

She said she chose not to telegraph what she called a very personal decision to step down, adding a recent change in the government’s assisted dying policies gave her the closure she needed.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced last week that the government will amend the Criminal Code to allow people to make advance requests for medical assistance in dying, also known as MAID.

Wallin has long advocated for advance directives after watching her mother’s long struggle with Alzheimer’s disease.

She’s been an outspoken supporter of MAID and served on multiple parliamentary committees that have studied the issue in recent years.

“I just think there are so many people in that situation that want to have some control and some sense of choice in the way that they leave, add some dignity to their departure,” she said.

Wallin said she leaves the Senate convinced that the institution is a “core part of our democracy,” although she believes the provinces should have much more say over who is appointed to represent them.

Albertans were voting Monday in a referendum that included a question about whether the government should work with other provinces to amend the Constitution to abolish the unelected Senate.

Wallin said that “until somebody comes up with some other genius idea,” the Senate is a critical way to ensure checks on the partisan House of Commons.

“The Senate itself is the only body that puts a second pair of eyes on crucial legislation, and our process is much more thoughtful and much more in-depth than the House has the opportunity to engage in,” she said.

Wallin’s time in the Senate followed a trail-blazing career as a journalist.

Wallin became a household name after being named co-host of Canada AM in 1981. She was tapped to lead CTV’s Ottawa bureau in 1985 — making her the first woman to head a national television news bureau in Canada — and was the producer and host of the network’s flagship political show Question Period.

She broke ground again in 1992 when she became the first woman to co-anchor a nightly news show in Canada — CBC’s Prime Time News.

Wallin had surgery for colorectal cancer in 2001 but continued a tour to promote her book at the time.

In 2002, she was named consul general to New York, just months after the 9/11 attacks, and served in that role for more than four years.

She was made an officer of the Order of Canada in 2007 and was appointed to the Senate in 2009 by Prime Minister Stephen Harper.

She became a key figure in the 2013 Senate expenses scandal after an audit found about $140,000 of the $500,000 in travel expenses she had billed to the Senate were improper because they were related to her work on corporate boards.

In May 2013, Harper’s chief of staff asked her to leave the Conservative caucus in the Senate.

During an interview with The National that year, Wallin apologized and said she did not “deliberately set out to use the system or abuse the system.”

She attributed the mistakes to carelessness in dealing with mounds of paperwork and said she didn’t pay enough attention to her expense filings.

In September, when she repaid some $150,000 — including interest — a defiant Wallin called out what she described as a “lynch mob” mentality in the Senate.

She was suspended without pay from the Senate in November 2013 over disallowed expenses, along with Mike Duffy and Patrick Brazeau.

Her Senate suspension was lifted when Parliament was dissolved for the 2015 election.

On Monday, Wallin said she had no interest in reliving that time but said the reforms that followed the expense scandal were necessary.

She has recently been a member of the Canadian Senators Group.

Speaking on behalf of the group, Sen. Flordeliz Osler said in a media statement that Wallin spent her career “asking difficult questions, challenging conventional thinking, and standing firmly behind her convictions.”

“From breaking barriers in Canadian journalism to representing Canada on the international stage and advocating passionately for the rights and dignity of Canadians in the Senate, she has never been one to shy away from difficult conversations,” said Osler.

“Her independence, determination and unmistakable voice have left a lasting mark on public life in Canada.”

Wallin, who is from Wadena, Sask., represented her home province in the Senate. She is two years shy of the mandatory retirement age of 75.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

items.title: Stelco posts strongest quarter amid layoffs at Nanticoke mill
items.description: The chief executive of Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. says Stelco has posted its strongest quarterly results since the Ohio-based company acquired the steelmaker.
items._ogDesc: The chief executive of Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. says Stelco has posted its strongest quarterly results since the Ohio-based company acquired the steelmaker.
items.body:
Stelco has posted its strongest quarterly results since Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. acquired the steelmaker two years ago, even as it moves ahead with up to 500 layoffs at its Ontario operations, chief executive Lourenco Goncalves said.

Stelco became a “positive contributor” to U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs’ third-quarter results for the period ended Sept. 30 amid a sharp improvement in Canada’s hot-rolled steel market, he said in an earnings release. 

However, Goncalves said more needs to be done by the Canadian government to correct “a clearly oversupplied market for galvanized steel in Canada.”

During an earnings call with analysts, he said the domestic market in Canada is not big enough to accommodate two Canadian producers of galvanized steel, Stelco and ArcelorMittal Dofasco, on top of what he called an “avalanche of imports.”

  • Latest updates on company news here

He said laid off workers could be brought back immediately if Ottawa brought in tighter import restrictions on galvanized steel.

“If the Canadian government uses the power they already have ... to block or severely reduce imports of galvanized steel into the Canadian market, Stelco can immediately bring back all the temporarily laid-off workers because that would immediately give us a market to sell and the ability to produce galvanized steel,” Goncalves said. 

He added that the Canadian government offered the steelmaker financial support, “but that’s not what Stelco needs.”

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

“What Stelco and Stelco workers really need is a market to sell galvanized steel, and government money cannot buy a market for galvanized steel.”

In the meantime, Goncalves said Stelco will concentrate on hot-rolled products “that actually have a market.”

He said total production tonnage at Stelco will be maintained, its contribution to Cleveland-Cliffs’ earnings will further increase, and about 2,000 Canadian jobs will be preserved.

Stelco produces hot-rolled steel at its Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont., for products such as construction materials and pipelines, while its Hamilton Works processes steel into cold-rolled and coated products, including galvanized steel, used for automotive, agriculture and infrastructure applications.

Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press

items.title: AI stocks lead a rebound on Wall Street as European markets drop following protests
items.description: Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry bounced back on Wall Street and recovered some of their steep losses from last week.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Fearless Girl statue stands in front of the New York Stock Exchange in New York's Financial District on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (AP Photo/Peter Morgan, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry bounced back on Wall Street and recovered some of their steep losses from last week.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry bounced back on Wall Street Monday and recovered some of their steep losses from last week, but the rest of the market and stocks worldwide were shaky.

The S&P 500 rose 0.4 per cent, coming off its worst week since June, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 1.1 per cent because it’s full of technology stocks. The majority of U.S. stocks outside of AI and tech fell, though, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average swung between losses and gains before finishing with a drop of 36 points, or 0.1 per cent.

In Europe, the losses were sharper, and indexes slid more than 1 per cent following violent protests that could ultimately force the French government to increase its spending to ease voters’ anger. That in turn could put even more pressure on bond markets, and yields cranked higher worldwide.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Even with all the cross currents flowing through financial markets, AI stocks stood out, as they have for most of the past few years. A frenzy in spending for AI technology has forced them to the forefront of the market, sending them to record prices and driving indexes higher. Last week, AI stocks grabbed the spotlight after tumbling on worries about how expensive it has become to borrow money, which could threaten the boom.

Much of the spending on AI chips and data centers has come from borrowed money, and Treasury yields in the bond market have recently hit their highest levels in years or even decades. That has raised the cost of borrowing money for everyone.

Nvidia added 1.4 per cent Monday and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total market value, a 1 per cent move for its stock has more effect on the index than any other’s.

SpaceX, which controls the xAI business, rose 1.3 per cent to US$147.96. Its founder, Elon Musk, pledged on Monday to give one share of SpaceX to “every kid in America” next year. The offer came after Anthropic said over the weekend that it will commit 5 per cent of the shares in its highly anticipated initial public offering of stock to a new “public benefit” fund.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The moves for AI stocks were still choppy, though. Consider CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud and has been at the center of the market’s swings. After initially jumping more than 7 per cent in the morning, it flipped to a loss of 3.5 per cent before finishing with a dip of 0.4 per cent. That followed its loss last week of 25.2 per cent.

The swings came ahead of profit reports coming later in the week that could offer more details about the strength of AI-related spending.

Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, will report its latest quarterly results on Wednesday. Lam Research, which supplies equipment and services for the making of semiconductors, will also talk about how its business is doing on Wednesday.

Expectations are high across the board for U.S. companies’ profits from the summer. Analysts are forecasting overall growth of 29 per cent for companies in the S&P 500 from the prior summer, according to FactSet. Those high expectations are what has allowed the U.S. stock market to run to records despite worries about war, high inflation and pressure from the bond market.

Cleveland-Cliffs rallied 16.3 per cent after reporting a bigger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Lourenco Goncalves said it was the strongest quarter for the company in three years and that the outlook for profit in 2027 “has improved materially” from three months ago.

All told, the S&P 500 rose 31.29 points to 7,690.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 36.38 to 51,966.03, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 290.85 to 26,430.89.

In stock markets abroad, rebounds for AI stocks helped South Korea’s Kospi jump 1.8 per cent to recover some of its 14.5 per cent drop from last week. It is dominated by two huge players in the AI industry, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which has made it much jumpier than other markets.

In Europe, bond yields climbed following the French protests against the rising cost of living and poor school conditions. The protests could put pressure on governments to boost their spending to offer help, but that would likely only add to their already big piles of debt.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Yields rose for French bonds on worries about the government’s already strained budget and climbed much more than yields for German government bonds, which investors have historically seen as a safer bet.

In the U.S. bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5.14 per cent from 5.09 per cent late Friday. It topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002.

Oil prices remained shaky. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, swung between US$107 and US$110 through the day before settling at US$109.55, down 0.3 per cent.

It has been yo-yoing between US$97 and US$110 this month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the energy industry to return to normal.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

items.title: Quebec's strategic maple syrup reserve running dry amid high demand
items.description: The head of Quebec’s maple syrup producer’s association says the province’s strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.
items.content:
<media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Cans of maple syrup wait to be processed at Érablière Coté et Fils in Roxton Pond, Que., on March 9, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Christinne Muschi
The Canadian Press]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Christinne Muschi</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The head of Quebec’s maple syrup producer’s association says the province’s strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.
items.body:
MONTRÉAL — The head of Quebec’s maple syrup producers’ association says the province’s strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.

Québec Maple Syrup Producers President Luc Goulet says government support will be needed to ensure the industry doesn’t miss out on opportunities to grow the sector.

Maple syrup yields depend on weather conditions.

As a result, the producers’ association has established a strategic reserve to ensure prices and supply remain relatively stable.

Last year, U.S. commercial customers stocked up, fearing that U.S. President Donald Trump would carry out his threat to impose tariffs.

Goulet says the buffer has been exhausted as sales continue to rise.

“Our strategic reserve has been reduced to zero,” Goulet said in an interview at the release of a report on the industry’s economic benefits. That means the industry could lose customers if weather conditions are less favourable for maple sap flow, he said.

Goulet cites the stock shortages in 2007 and 2008 as an example.

“We lost some markets because the product wasn’t available,” Goulet said. “Then, consumers very quickly turn to another sweet product. And once that happens, those consumption habits are established.”

Quebec maple syrup is gaining market share abroad, according to the president of the Maple Industry Council, which represents authorized buyers.

Louis Turenne notes that exports increased by 9.34 per cent in 2024 compared to the previous year. The pace accelerated in 2025 with a 15.8 per cent increase as the threat of new tariffs loomed over the industry.

In 2026, exports rose at a slower rate — 2.48 per cent from January through August compared to the same period the previous year. “It’s always hard to beat an exceptional year,” Turenne said.

Goulet acknowledges that satisfying the demand of eager consumers is a nice problem to have. However, he believes the industry can still grow. “There is still a great deal of untapped potential in Quebec’s maple groves,” he said.

Investments from Quebec City “are too low for our liking,” says Goulet, who hopes to have the ear of the newly-elected Parti Québécois government.

“When we’re told that we have an industry that’s thriving, that we’re growing, and that we don’t need support — well, I no longer accept that line of reasoning at the government level,” he said.

For his part, Turenne believes that Quebec could encourage increased production by providing financial support to producers, and helping processors in their search for new markets abroad.

Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States. “We’ve made significant progress in diversifying our markets in recent years. Twenty years ago, that figure was 80 per cent,” Turenne said.

“But we need to accelerate the opening and development of European, Australian, and Asian markets to become less dependent on the U.S. market,” he said.

While the maple leaf graces the Canadian flag, the syrup industry is heavily concentrated in Quebec. More than 70 per cent of North American production is in the province, according to the industry group’s report, released Thursday.

When production, processing, and specialized equipment manufacturers are included, the maple syrup industry contributed $1.21 billion to the gross domestic product in 2025, the report said.

In total, the sector employs more than 10,000 full-time equivalent workers and generated $285 million in tax revenue, excluding municipal taxes and fees for the lease of public lands.

This figure does not include the sugar shacks that many Quebecers visit in the spring.

“Sugar shack operations are more akin to the restaurant industry,” Turenne said.

The maple syrup producers’ group used the recent election campaign to highlight the industry’s importance as an employer and economic driver, and Goulet says the candidates were often surprised by the important role it played.

In some municipalities, “if you take away maple syrup production, you might as well shut down the villages,” Goulet said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

The post Canadian Inflation Accelerates, Only 2 Provinces Below National CPI appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: September Canadian inflation breached the BoC target at 3.1%. Regional CPI data reveals only Ontario and BC are below the national average.
items.body:
The August Consumer Price Index (CPI) report breached the Bank of Canada (BoC) upper bound. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows CPI accelerated further in September. A regional breakdown reveals that only two provinces are below the national average. Headline growth is well above the BoC’s target rate, but some provinces have more than doubled that rate.

Canadian Inflation Accelerates, Already Past BoC Upper Bound

Canadian CPI annual growth.

Annual growth of CPI accelerated to 3.1% in September, up from 3.0% in August. The outsized impact of soaring gas prices continues, with CPI ex-gasoline at just 2.2% over the same period. The agency further notes that only 3 of 8 major components saw prices accelerate too.

The headline data makes it easy to conclude this is only an energy story. However, a regional breakdown of CPI makes it clear that basket distortions are in play. Only two provinces have seen a rate lower than the national average.

Atlantic Provinces Over 2x BoC Target, Only 2 Provinces Below Average

Despite being above the Bank of Canada (BoC) upper bound of 3.0%, CPI may be skewed by its modelling. A quick look at the provincial breakdowns, and we see Ontario (+2.5%) is the only province below the threshold. Add BC (+3.0%) to the mix, and we get the only two provinces lower than the national average. The rest of Canada isn’t quite this lucky—especially out east.

CPI’s highest growth is almost exclusively concentrated in Atlantic Canada. PEI’s annual growth of 5.7%—approaching triple the BoC’s target of 2%—is the highest in the country. Not far behind are Nova Scotia (+5.6%), New Brunswick (+5.0%), and Newfoundland and Labrador (+4.7%). The Prairies aren’t much better off either—Manitoba (+4.4%), Alberta (+3.6%), and Saskatchewan (+3.3%) are above the national average too.

It’s not just gas, either. CPI ex-gasoline remained elevated in Nova Scotia (+4.4%), PEI (+3.9%), and New Brunswick (+3.4%). The agency separately notes “… rent prices rose the fastest in Atlantic Canada,” which can help explain some of the distortion.

Energy and Shelter Are Among The Biggest Drivers of CPI

The biggest driver of annual growth remains energy, with 19% annual growth. The sector is driven by a 27.8% surge in gas, along with a 57.8% jump in fuel oil. Considering energy is an input cost for everything, its surprising growth isn’t broad.

Shelter accelerated 1.8%, driven by home/mortgage insurance (+4.9%) and rent (+2.8%). The sector was moderated by falling replacement costs (-1.9%), tied to the cost of building new homes. It was dragged further by mortgage interest (-0.2%), which is likely to be news to brokers considering yields.

In short, Canada’s headline inflation is running hot—and the national average is weak in contrast to what most households are experiencing.

items.title: What Canada's latest inflation reading means for mortgages
items.description: Could September’s CPI data impact the BoC’s next decision on October 28?
items.content: <p>Could September’s CPI data impact the BoC’s next decision on October 28?</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639280340084394431.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Could September’s CPI data impact the BoC’s next decision on October 28?
items.body:
Canada’s annual inflation rate came in at 3.1% last month, a reading that some experts believe could keep the Bank of Canada on hold when it meets next week.

The consumer price index (CPI) climbed slightly over August, according to new Statistics Canada data, but analysts including Dominion Lending Centres Group (DLCG) chief economist Sherry Cooper say the rise likely wasn’t enough to justify an October hike.

“The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting,” Cooper said this morning. “Policymakers will continue to closely monitor incoming inflation data and stand ready to tighten policy if price pressures broaden and become more persistent.

“Still, for now, underlying inflation trends in Canada remain consistent with a patient, wait-and-see approach.”

Latest inflation reading ‘good news’: economist

A rate hold by the Bank of Canada would mean no change for variable mortgage rates, although five-year Government of Canada bond yields – which heavily influence fixed rates – have continued an unpredictable path and whipsawed over the past five days.

Those yields had ticked slightly higher at time of writing on Monday afternoon compared with the same time yesterday.

Still, National Bank of Canada (NBC) chief economist Stéfane Marion, speaking in a keynote address at the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary, described the latest inflation reading as a positive one for the mortgage market.

“Good news this morning – inflation came out, it’s not dramatic,” he said. “Core inflation is still at 2%. I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive.”

CPA Canada chief economist David-Alexandre Brassard also sees the latest reading keeping rate hikes off the table this month. “For now, there is still no clear-cut reason for the Bank of Canada to move interest rates in either direction, as both risks [a weakening economy and rising inflation] are working against one another,” Brassard said.

And he hinted that a further dramatic spike in rates looks unlikely at this stage. “I think most of the increase that we’ve seen in interest rates is behind us,” he said. “And if we’re right, it sets the stage for a normalization going into next year.”

Inflation on the rise, but sluggish economy isn’t picking up

While inflation has been ticking upwards in recent months, the economy has remained sluggish – with some forecasts indicating a further slowdown could be in store.

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB), which represents 103,000 small and medium-sized firms, said in its latest Main Street Quarterly report that it sees Canada’s overall GDP growth slowing again in the fourth quarter.

The latest inflation increase was spurred, unsurprisingly, by another surge in fuel oil and other fuel costs, which soared by 57.8% amid continuing price pressures from the war in Iran.

Homeowners’ home and mortgage insurance costs rose by 4.9% compared with the same time last year, while homeowners’ maintenance and repairs costs also moved higher (by 1.2%).

For now, the rate outlook remains uncertain for scores of buyers, particularly with the mortgage renewal wave still going strong.

Speaking with Canadian Mortgage Professional, Haventree Bank president and chief executive officer Fern Glowinsky (pictured below) said mortgage brokers are coming to the fore in that environment.

“I think if there’s a good option in front of the borrower right now for a longer period of time, that’s a good call,” she said. “I think if you can find an offer that lines up with affordability and structure for you that takes you through this period of uncertainty, it’s probably a good idea – because over time, things will settle down.”

items.title: Foreign homebuyer ban should be revised, says NBC’s Marion
items.description: National Bank economist calls for foreign buyer ban revision as unsold condos hit a 30-year high
items.content: <p>National Bank economist calls for foreign buyer ban revision as unsold condos hit a 30-year high</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639280326776111776.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: National Bank economist calls for foreign buyer ban revision as unsold condos hit a 30-year high
items.body:
With additional reporting by Fergal McAlinden

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada (NBC), has called on the federal government to revise the country’s ban on non-resident foreign homebuyers, arguing the restriction directly undermines Ottawa’s drive to restore Canada’s appeal to international investors.

Speaking at the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary on Tuesday, Marion said he expects Ottawa to act before the ban’s January 1, 2027 expiry — and that any revision should specifically permit foreign nationals to purchase new-build homes.

He framed the call around a striking market figure: 28% of newly constructed condominiums are currently unsold, a level he said is the highest since the early 1990s.

“How can you pretend to be a standout investor again if you tell foreign buyers you can’t touch the residential market in Canada?” Marion said.

“I think they’re going to revise this at a time where 28% of condos that they built are not absorbed, which is the highest proportion we’ve seen since the early 1990s. So against this backdrop, I would certainly expect to see some modification to allow foreigners to buy into new build, and that fits the overall message of making Canada investable again.”

Those views align with a growing chorus across the industry. Don Kottick, president of RE/MAX Canada, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this month that the ban has actively suppressed the very supply the market needs.

“I think if you look at the foreign buyer ban and the negative impact that it had on preconstruction, it took a lot of money out of the market that would have driven more preconstruction, more units coming on the market,” Kottick said.

“So hopefully, if that is removed in January, we start to see more investment coming back, which could drive affordability.” 

Kottick was equally direct on government intervention more broadly. “We’ve had governments that have always tried to bring policy. Policy will never fix the market,” he said.

“Hopefully the government has learned a lesson that natural market forces have been more beneficial than any government policy — because there’s always been unintended consequences.”

The remarks add a prominent voice to a debate that has gathered pace in recent months. Industry pressure for a new-build exemption has been building as the ban’s January 2027 expiry approaches, particularly among developers and pre-sale brokers.

The decision Ottawa makes before year-end ranks among the most consequential housing policy calls it faces in 2026.

Demographic slowdown and the immigration reset

Marion was equally pointed on immigration. Canada moved from roughly 1.2 million newcomers annually at its recent peak to approximately 200,000, a near-collapse in inflows that has weighed heavily on demand across Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec, where population growth has effectively stalled.

“We went from going to 1.2 million people a year a couple years ago to a dramatic slowdown, just 200,000,” he said.

“At most it’s 300,000 — that’s what the system can cope with. Negative population growth is not the solution either.”

He highlighted Canada’s long-term demographic advantage. The country remains the only jurisdiction globally projecting no population decline through 2066, a structural foundation, he argued, that underpins long-term housing demand even amid near-term disruption.

Broker implications and the 2027 stabilization forecast

Marion projected the national composite index — down 4% in 2026 — to level off by 2027, supported by labour shortages and construction cost pressures that limit the downside.

For brokers, the broader deregulation agenda Marion outlined may prove as relevant as any single housing policy shift.

“I am the most optimistic I’ve been over a decade,” he said.

items.title: Bank of Canada’s next move: what top economists are saying
items.description: Canada’s top bank economists have weighed in on October 28 after Tuesday’s CPI release
items.content: <p>Canada’s top bank economists have weighed in on October 28 after Tuesday’s CPI release</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639280217704442110.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s top bank economists have weighed in on October 28 after Tuesday’s CPI release
items.body:
Four economists from Canada’s largest financial institutions are calling a Bank of Canada rate hold at the October 28 meeting in Ottawa, after September’s consumer price index (CPI) landed below market consensus and the Bank’s preferred core measures averaged 1.9% year-over-year.

The consensus is patience, but not without a dissenting voice on timing.

What economists are saying about the October 28 rate decision

Leslie Preston, Managing Director and Senior Economist at TD Economics in Canada, set the tone.

“No jump scares in Canada’s inflation in September, in contrast to higher inflation south of the border,” she wrote.

“Today’s number supports our view that the Bank of Canada can remain on hold this year. There is little evidence higher energy costs are bleeding through to broader price pressures, which remain mild.” 

Abbey Xu, economist at RBC Economics in Toronto, flagged a more cautious signal from Governor Tiff Macklem himself.

Xu noted that Macklem, speaking at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, warned “the risk that inflation broadens and becomes more persistent has gone up,” and that the Bank has found it increasingly difficult to look through the direct impact of higher energy prices.

RBC’s base case holds the overnight rate at 2.25% through year-end before rising modestly in 2027.

Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC in Toronto, went further, noting that bond yields moved before Tuesday’s release on the back of Macklem’s weekend remarks.

“It’s possible that a first interest rate hike could come earlier than the January move we previously forecast,” he said. 

Dr. Sherry Cooper, Chief Economist at Dominion Lending Centres in Canada, read the September data as confirmation that energy is not yet spreading into broader price growth.

“Today’s inflation report reinforces our view that higher gasoline prices temporarily boost headline inflation while further eroding household purchasing power. However, these energy-driven increases, largely tied to geopolitical tensions, are unlikely to trigger a broader resurgence in underlying inflation,” she said.

On the Bank’s next move, Cooper was direct: “The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting. Policymakers will continue to closely monitor incoming inflation data and stand ready to tighten policy if price pressures broaden and become more persistent. Still, for now, underlying inflation trends in Canada remain consistent with a patient, wait-and-see approach.”

Behind the September CPI numbers

Statistics Canada’s September report showed headline CPI at 3.1% year-over-year, above August’s 3.0% but below the 3.2% consensus estimate.

Gasoline prices surged 27.8% year-over-year from 22.8% in August, as crude oil reached its highest level since May.

Grocery store prices rose 1.7% year-over-year, the slowest pace since May 2024, down from 2.8% in August.

Shelter inflation ticked to 1.8% from 1.5%, driven by fuel oil costs and higher homeowners’ insurance premiums.

The Bank of Canada’s preferred core gauges — CPI-trim and CPI-median — averaged 1.9% year-over-year, slipping below August’s 2.0% and below the Bank’s own 2% inflation target.

items.content: <p>Core inflation eases to 1.9% as energy prices drive the headline</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639280143870576555.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Core inflation eases to 1.9% as energy prices drive the headline
items.body:
Canada’s annual inflation rate climbed to 3.1% in September, up from 3.0% in August, according to Statistics Canada data released Monday — and economists say the reading gives the Bank of Canada (BoC) little reason to lift its overnight rate at the October 28 meeting.

Energy drove nearly all of the acceleration. Gasoline prices surged 27.8% year over year, up from 22.8% in August, as crude oil reached its highest level since May amid ongoing Middle East conflict.

Broader energy costs rose 19.0% annually, following a 15.4% gain the prior month. Excluding energy entirely, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose just 2.2%.

Core pressures stay contained

For mortgage brokers advising clients on rate timing, the more instructive signal came from the BoC’s preferred core measures.

CPI-median fell to 1.9% in September from 2.0% in August, while CPI-trim eased to 1.8% from 1.9%, both moving away from hike territory and averaging 1.9% across the two, down from 2.0% the month prior.

Leslie Preston, managing director and senior economist at TD Economics in Toronto, offered a clear verdict.

“No jump scares in Canada’s inflation in September,” she said.

“There is little evidence higher energy costs are bleeding through to broader price pressures, which remain mild. Today’s number supports our view that the Bank of Canada can remain on hold this year.”

That view aligns with analysis from Abbey Xu, economist at Royal Bank of Canada in Toronto, who found limited evidence that elevated energy costs were generating significant second-round inflation in her reading of August’s data, a conclusion September’s numbers do nothing to challenge.

Grocery prices also moderated further. Food purchased from stores rose 1.7% year over year in September, the smallest annual gain since May 2024, down from 2.8% in August.

Shelter prices edged up 1.8%, with rent rising 2.8%.

Don Kottick of RE/MAX Canada says buyers remain willing to make compromises, from relocating farther from city centres to adjusting their spending habits, to achieve their homeownership goals. https://t.co/GOHrsHlsWY — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 14, 2026

What October 28 means for brokers

The September CPI release is the last major data point before the October 28 decision, which will be accompanied by a full Monetary Policy Report.

As CMP reported following Canada’s September labour market shock, a deteriorating jobs picture had already pulled near-term hike expectations sharply lower.

Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union in Edmonton, described the Governing Council’s bind plainly.

“We believe it will opt for patience,” he said.

“As a result, we think the BoC will keep its policy rate unchanged for the rest of the year, unless there are signs in the CPI data of a broadening of inflation.”

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres (DLC) in Vancouver, pointed directly to Monday’s release: “The Bank of Canada will likely hold off on a rate hike, especially if the inflation data released on October 19 brings no nasty surprises.”

With the overnight rate at 2.25%, held across eight consecutive meetings, mortgage professionals navigating client conversations ahead of the October 28 BoC decision now have their clearest signal yet.

As Leah Zlatkin, a licensed mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, has cautioned: “There’s no clear signal that rates are heading materially lower, and in some cases we’re already seeing lenders adjust pricing upward.” October 28 looks unlikely to change that.

items.title: Christopher Liew: Which accounts should you draw from first in retirement?
items.description: Personal finance contributor Christopher Liew walks through which accounts he'd advice drawing from first in retirement, and when he’d consider breaking the rules.
items._ogDesc: Personal finance contributor Christopher Liew walks through which accounts he'd advice drawing from first in retirement, and when he’d consider breaking the rules.
items.body:
Christopher Liew is a CFP®, CFA Charterholder and former financial advisor. He writes personal finance tips for thousands of daily Canadian readers at Blueprint Financial.

You spent decades filling up your RRSP, your TFSA, and maybe a non-registered account. Now that retirement is here (or close), you have to figure out how to empty them, and the order could matter more than you might think.

Pull from the wrong account at the wrong time and you could hand the CRA far more than you need to, or see part of your Old Age Security clawed back.

Below, I’ll walk through which accounts I’d typically draw from first, and when I’d break the rules.

Why the order you withdraw in matters

Earlier this year, I wrote about the wrong ways to save for retirement. Spending that money well is just as important, and not having a withdrawal plan was one of the common financial regrets of retirees I flagged in June.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The classic rule of thumb is non-registered first, then RRSP or RRIF, then TFSA last. It’s a decent starting point, but in my experience the best plans blend accounts year by year rather than draining them one at a time. With year-end approaching, it’s also a good moment to check how much taxable income you’ve already earned in 2026, since anything you withdraw before Dec. 31 lands on this year’s return.

1. Start with your non-registered account

Money in a regular taxable account is the least sheltered dollar you own. Interest, dividends, and realized gains get taxed every year, even if you’re just reinvesting, so this account loses a slice of its return to tax drag annually. Spending it first lets your sheltered accounts keep compounding.

That being said, watch your capital gains. If your investments have grown a lot, try to sell in your lower-income years, ideally before you start collecting OAS. Only half of a capital gain is taxable, but that half still counts toward your net income. I’d also keep a modest cash cushion here for emergencies rather than draining the account to zero.

2. Don’t always leave your RRSP untouched until 71

I often see retirees leave their RRSP alone until they’re forced to convert it to a RRIF at the end of the year they turn 71.

Instead, consider a bracket-filling approach. In the years between retiring and 71, you could withdraw enough to bring your income to the top of a lower tax bracket without spilling into the next one. This smooths your taxes, shrinks future forced withdrawals, and reduces your estate’s tax bill, since a RRIF is generally taxed in full on your final return unless it rolls to a spouse.

At 65, it’s also worth converting part of your RRSP to a RRIF. Those payments qualify for the pension income amount, a federal credit on up to $2,000 of eligible income, and can be split with your spouse on your tax returns to help keep both incomes under the OAS recovery tax threshold for 2026. I walked through this with actual numbers in a recent Blueprint Financial video.

3. Consider using RRSP withdrawals to buy time on CPP and OAS

Early RRSP withdrawals could also pair nicely with delaying your government pensions. CPP payments rise by 0.7 per cent for each month you wait past 65, up to 42 per cent more at 70. OAS offers a smaller but similar boost if you defer it.

Living off your RRSP in your 60s while you wait essentially swaps a taxable account for bigger, inflation-indexed income for life. I think it’s one of the most underrated moves in Canadian retirement planning. It isn’t for everyone, though; if your health is poor or your savings are thin, starting earlier can make more sense.

4. Treat your TFSA as a flexible reserve, not just the last stop

Your TFSA is the most flexible account you have. The CRA confirms your OAS and Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) won’t be reduced by TFSA income or withdrawals. That makes it the ideal source of cash in a year when you’re near the clawback, selling a property, or facing a big one-time expense.

It’s also your best buffer in a down market, since you can spend from it instead of selling RRIF investments at a loss. And if your RRSP withdrawals exceed what you spend, move the extra into your TFSA, if you have room, so it grows tax-free from here on.

If you expect to qualify for GIS, I’d go further and move the TFSA to the front of the line, since keeping taxable income low is what protects that benefit.

5. Fit your other income around the plan

If you have a defined benefit pension or an annuity, treat it as your income floor. Then plan your RRSP or RRIF withdrawals around it so you stay in your target tax bracket. Rental income works the same way, and in a year with big repairs or a vacancy, your TFSA can cover the gap.

If you own a business with money in a corporation, you have extra levers, like timing dividends for your lower-income years.

Your home is your last-resort safety valve. A home equity line of credit set up while you still qualify can cover short-term needs in a down market, so you don’t have to sell investments at a loss. A reverse mortgage comes with higher interest and fees, so I’d use it selectively, usually later in life to fund care or stay in your home longer.

Final thoughts

There’s no single withdrawal order that works for everyone. Your pensions, health, spouse, and estate goals all shift the answer, and the right mix usually changes from year to year. What matters is having a plan before you start pulling money out, rather than letting the RRIF rules make the decisions for you. A few hours of planning now could save you thousands later.

items.description: Beem's Brian Harris urges greater emphasis on financial behaviour
items._ogDesc: Beem's Brian Harris urges greater emphasis on financial behaviour
items.body:
With housing costs and living expenses remaining high in B.C., people struggling to save for a down payment shouldn't be shut out of homeownership, says the CEO of a major credit union.

Brian Harris, president and CEO of Beem Credit Union, said down payments have become an “outdated” primary measure of a person’s readiness for homeownership, an argument that at least one housing expert disputes.

“If you think about the fact that people are saving money anywhere from three to nine years to get into homeownership, that's a lot of money tied up in rental that could have otherwise been much more constructively used,” said Harris.

“I just think it's a really outdated way of determining worthiness and readiness for homeownership.”

About one-third (32 per cent) of Canadians said saving for a down payment was their main barrier to entering the housing market, according to a 2025 survey by CPA Canada and BDO Debt Solutions.

A September survey by Royal LePage also found that more than half of the 1,400 newcomers surveyed across Canada cited saving for a down payment as their biggest barrier for homeownership.

Harris said a family in Metro Vancouver could pay $5,000 a month in rent—an amount that could be comparable to the monthly mortgage payment on a home worth roughly $1 million, depending on the financing terms.

Rather than using down payment as a predominant criterion, Harris said lenders could take a more thoughtful and creative approach to evaluating mortgage applicants by considering their credit history, spending habits and track record of rental payment.

“We have consumer-directed finance, or open banking, as it’s more affectionately referred to, coming to Canada, so we have the ability in the very near term to have really good data insights to determine how somebody is spending their money,” he said.

Canada’s consumer-driven banking framework is designed to allow consumers to share their financial data securely with accredited third-party providers of their choice. The federal government has established the legislative framework and is developing supporting regulations to put it into operation.

“There's a real opportunity for us to use demonstrated behaviours and other sort of support tools to get people in [if] they've exhibited good financial behaviours,” said Harris.

He said a more flexible approach to mortgage qualification could also benefit the broader housing market by matching the demand for homeownership with accessibility.

“I think it's got a lot of great knock-on effects. It gets people who are renting into whatever form it takes, a small home, a condo, a townhouse, whatever it might be,” said Harris.

“But it then also frees up the rental market for those who are not yet ready to buy their own home.”

Down payment requirements still matter

While a down payment is not the only indicator of someone’s readiness for homeownership, removing the requirement could increase risks for both lenders and buyers, according to one real estate expert.

“The benefits of having a down payment, both in terms of an indication that the borrower's capable of making ongoing payments or de-risking the loan for the lender, I think are still true,” said Thomas Davidoff, an associate professor and director for UBC Centre for Urban Economics and Real Estate.

He said one of the main benefits of requesting a down payment is that it makes it harder for the buyer to get to a situation where the property is worth less than what the borrower owes, so they may walk away and stop paying the mortgage.

The ability to save for a down payment remains an important indicator of a person’s capability to save, alongside a good credit history, he said. However, he acknowledged that it is harder than it used to be to save for a down payment due to housing affordability issues in the region.

“If the money comes from the parents, less so, but on the other hand … that indicates you have [supportive] parents, which is helpful,” he said.

A down payment also reduces the amount a buyer needs to borrow, lowering monthly mortgage payments and borrowing costs, Davidoff added.

In addition, the current housing downturn indicates that property prices could fall, making high loan-to-value mortgages riskier, he said.

The key to tackling housing affordability is not in changing mortgage qualification rules, but lies in increasing the supply and growing the economy to boost people’s incomes and purchasing power, according to Davidoff.

“Higher earnings, more houses, that's the recipe,” he said.

“Make sure people are more able to earn a strong income with better education and a stronger labour market, more employers, so things like trade diversification in the face of U.S. tariffs, anything like that helps.”

items.title: The strategic side to alternative lending
items.description: Calvert Home Mortgage Investment Corporation on why the savviest brokers start with the exit, not the rate
items.content: <p>Calvert Home Mortgage Investment Corporation on why the savviest brokers start with the exit, not the rate</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639257040480876337.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Calvert Home Mortgage Investment Corporation on why the savviest brokers start with the exit, not the rate
items.body:
Mortgage brokers have no shortage of lender options. More choice should make finding a mortgage solution easier, however, for many brokers, it can have the opposite effect.

Every lender comes with different products, pricing, guidelines, and nuances. Add alternative lenders into the mix, and the challenge isn't just knowing who will fund a deal. It's knowing when to use which option and why.

Private and alternative lending was once seen primarily as a last resort. Today there's a growing opportunity for Mortgage Brokers to leverage this flexibility more strategically to solve timing, preserve favorable existing financing, access equity, or give the client the time they need to reach their next step.

That's an important distinction in alternative lending, where financing may only be needed for a few months, or even a few weeks. For Mortgage Brokers, the real opportunity is understanding what the client is trying to accomplish and then looking at the numbers in that context.

Maybe a real estate investor has found the right property but needs to close quickly. A homeowner could have plenty of equity but needs another year before they're ready to refinance conventionally. Or a client may already have a great first mortgage they don't want to give up but needs access to additional capital.

This is where Calvert Home Mortgage Investment Corporation believes mortgage brokers can bring more strategy to the conversation.

Start with the exit

These aren't necessarily clients who need a permanent alternative mortgage. They may just need the right financing for this particular moment.

This is where starting with the exit becomes critical to the solution. The client’s end goal, how long they need the financing and what needs to happen next should all influence how the deal is structured.

A four-month plan can become six months. A sale can take longer than expected. A refinance can be delayed. Building flexibility into the financing from the start can help keep a temporary solution from becoming an expensive one. When the financing supports the client’s bigger goal, everyone wins: the client has a clearer path forward and the broker builds a relationship that can extend well beyond one deal.

The real cost of financing

Comparing an alternative mortgage rate directly with a conventional rate doesn't always tell the full story. How long the financing is needed, how it's structured and what it allows the client to accomplish all matter.

If financing is only needed for four months, for example, what will it actually cost over those four months? And what could waiting for a lower-rate option mean for the client's plans?

For a real estate investor, moving quickly could mean securing the right property or completing renovations in time to refinance or sell. For a homeowner, short-term financing could bridge the timing gap between buying and selling, or provide the flexibility needed to transition to traditional financing.

Calvert Home Mortgage has built its approach around flexibility, creative problem-solving and strong mortgage broker partnerships, with teams working together to uncover opportunities within a deal, whether that means structuring a blanket mortgage, preserving an existing first mortgage or finding another way to make the numbers work for the client's next step.

Structure can change the numbers too. A client with an attractive first mortgage may be better served by keeping it in place and adding a short-term second rather than refinancing the entire balance. Looking at the blended cost overall can give the mortgage broker and client a much more useful comparison than looking at the second mortgage rate on its own or at refinancing an entire mortgage.

“A good mortgage broker isn’t just finding their client a mortgage for today. They’re thinking about where that client needs to be six months, a year or two years from now,” says Jesse Bobrowski, VP of Growth at Calvert Home Mortgage. “Our role is to work alongside our partners, bring our lending experience to the conversation and help find a path that gets their client where they want to go.”

Putting alternative lending to work

As the real estate and mortgage markets become more challenging, straightforward deals may be harder to come by. For mortgage brokers, that makes the ability to solve more complex needs more valuable.

Using alternative lending strategically doesn’t mean knowing every product or guideline. It means recognizing when a different approach could help and having a lending partner who can work through the options with you.

At Calvert Home Mortgage, we want brokers to bring us the story. What is the client trying to do? What’s getting in the way? And where do they want to go?

“In this market, you’re not going to win every deal with the obvious solution,” says Jesse Bobrowski, VP of Growth at Calvert Home Mortgage Investment Corporation. “Sometimes you need a lender who’s willing to dig in, ask questions and look for another way forward.”

The best mortgage brokers don’t have every answer. They have the right partners to help find one. In a competitive market, that ability to find a way forward is what sets them apart.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada’s Housing Crash Rivals US In 2008, But The Pain Is Hidden: BMO

The Canadian housing crash now rivals the US in 2008, with prices falling for nearly 5 years. However, unlike the US crash, Canada’s economy appears to have avoided most of the negatives. The country’s economy grew 1.7% annually over the four years, helped by stronger borrowers and rate cuts. Strong headline data is hiding the true impact, warns BMO Capital Markets. That strong GDP growth is actually negative when adjusted per capita. Meanwhile, resilient consumption is due to a reliance on seniors, who aren’t impacted by a rise in unemployment so sharp it’s rarely seen outside of recessions. The economy is in turmoil, the optics are just focused on the wrong areas.

Canadian Real Estate Spent 5 Years Wiping Out Just 13 Months of Gains

Canadian home prices fell 0.9% (-$5.7k) to $651,400 in September, 22.5% (-$189k) lower than the March 2022 peak. Home prices are now down to February 2021 levels, a timeline worth some attention. The painful market correction that’s lasted almost 5 years has only managed to wipe out 13 months of gains. Historically weak sales and near-record high inventory suggest the downturn isn’t over.

Canadian Bond Yields & Borrowing Rates To Rise With US Inflation: BMO

Borrowing in Canada is set to get more expensive due to rising US inflation. Canada’s 2-year government bond yield rose to 3.25% this week, and the Bank of Canada is expected to hike 1 point by 2027. Yields were driven by higher gas prices, but continued to climb even after gas prices stopped. BMO warns Canada’s yields are rising due to US inflation, despite domestic weaknesses.

Canadians Plan To Buy First Home At 41, Property Ladder Breaks: RBC

Canadians plan to enter the housing market at a much later age in life than past generations. A new survey from RBC found the average first-time buyer plans to buy at 41 years old, 12 years later than usual. Being older with higher incomes, they plan to skip starters and want a long-term purchase. At the same time, nearly half of the owners who want to upgrade can’t actually afford to in this market. This combination can mean the end of the property ladder, and a big change for the real estate industry.

items.title: Potential BoC rate hikes loom over Canada’s housing market outlook
items.description: Homebuyers might normally be tempted to enter the market to get ahead of rate increases – but that’s not happening, says Royal LePage CEO
items.content: <p>Homebuyers might normally be tempted to enter the market to get ahead of rate increases – but that’s not happening, says Royal LePage CEO</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639278467518790697.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Homebuyers might normally be tempted to enter the market to get ahead of rate increases – but that’s not happening, says Royal LePage CEO
items.body:
The Bank of Canada is still expected to hold rates steady at its next meeting on October 28, but financial markets are pricing in an increasing likelihood that the central bank will start hiking in the months ahead amid continuing concerns about the inflation outlook.

While a sluggish labour market looks set to tip the balance in favour of another BoC hold at the end of the month, experts don’t see that wait-and-see approach lasting for long.

Dominion Lending Centres Group (DLCG) chief economist Sherry Cooper suggested a rate increase could arrive as soon as December 9, the Bank’s last scheduled rate decision of the year, as global pressure gathers for central banks to take a more aggressive stand on inflation.

The BoC’s benchmark rate, which strongly influences variable Canadian mortgage rates, has remained unchanged throughout the year to date. But fixed rates have been climbing in recent weeks, reflecting jitters in global bond markets and adding further complications for mortgage shoppers.

A rate increase by the US Federal Reserve in its last decision also sparked speculation that Canada’s central bank could be set to follow suit soon.

Rising rates are tempering already subdued expectations for the housing market. On Friday, the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) slashed its 2026 home sales forecast for the third consecutive quarter, while TD has also revised its own outlook.

Why potential homebuyers aren’t pushing ahead

The looming possibility of Bank of Canada rate hikes might sometimes spur potential homebuyers into action because their borrowing costs could be much higher if they wait for a few months.

Amid the current economic uncertainty, that doesn’t appear to be the case, according to Royal LePage president and chief executive officer Phil Soper (pictured top). He told Canadian Mortgage Professional that would-be buyers still appear to prefer sitting on the sidelines because they’re nervous about the US-Canada trade war and rising inflation.  

“You’d expect with lots of chatter about rate increases in Canada online bubbling through communities – plus the recent significant rise in fixed-rate mortgages in the United States – that there’d be some pull-ahead in activity,” Soper said. “You’d see some people that were planning to get into the market in the spring of 2027, for example, jumping in now to get ahead of anticipated higher borrowing costs.

“Yet we’re not seeing material changes in the trajectory of transaction volumes. It’s very flat. And what that says to me is even an incentive like that is not enough to get people off the sidelines if they’re feeling very uncomfortable.”

Soper: Fundamentals in place for healthy market, but Canadians remain nervous

Royal LePage now expects a more modest pace of national 2026 home price growth than it first anticipated. In its second-quarter house price survey, the real estate firm said prices would likely jump by 2% by Q4 – but it’s revised that to 1%, reflecting the deep freeze that still grips the market.

Major markets including Toronto and Vancouver saw prices continue to slide in the second quarter, according to Royal LePage, although other cities including Montreal bucked the national trend.

Soper suggested meaningful change in the housing market outlook might not arrive unless positive news emerges on the trade war, which has seen the US and Canada exchange a flurry of tariffs and counter-tariffs on products crossing the border.

“It doesn’t seem that anything will budge Canadians from their rigor mortis while this trade war is raging with the United States,” he said. “What I mean by that is we’ve got pent-up demand, we’ve got reasonable mortgage rates, we’ve got lower home prices, employment’s reasonable and steady, and savings are high.

“All the fundamentals are in place for a much more active housing market, but our research shows first-time homebuyers in particular are just so nervous about the trade war, and in particular Donald Trump’s behaviour and what it might mean to Canada and ultimately to them, that they are sitting on the sidelines and waiting.”
